corrected_value.authors: Ogden, R., Makin, A. D. J., Palumbo, L., & Bertamini, M.
corrected_value.title: Symmetry lasts longer than random, but only for brief presentations

decisions.location: Discussion, line 39 (see also Introduction, lines 6-8; Discussion, lines 43-44; References, line 64)
decisions.quote: Despite our predictions, there was no evidence that symmetrical dot patterns were judged longer than random dot patterns, and no evidence that this effect was further modulated by the number of folds. The basic effect of symmetry on subjective duration already reported by Palumbo et al. (2015), Ogden et al. (2016) and Sasaki and Yamada (2017) was not replicated.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists. The source paper collects new empirical data (N=40 in a 2 Regularity x 5 Folds x 3 Duration within-subjects design plus filler trials) to re-test the published finding that reflectional symmetry elongates subjective duration relative to random patterns in brief presentations. It explicitly details Ogden et al.'s (2016) Experiment 1 (500-1500 ms checkerboards, F(2,42)=17.114, p<0.001, partial eta-squared=0.451) and Experiment 2 (temporal bisection), tests reflection vs. random patterns across sub-second durations (0.4, 0.6, 0.8 s), finds no effect of Regularity (F<1), and directly compares its results and duration effect size (partial eta-squared=0.85 vs. Ogden et al. 2016 partial eta-squared=0.88) in the Discussion, concluding that Ogden et al. (2016) was not replicated. Full bibliographic identity including DOI 10.1177/2041669516676824 is verified in the reference list (line 64) and Crossref metadata. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2413) is Sasaki and Yamada (2017, DOI 10.1177/2041669517728944), an independent study by a Waseda University team using regularity grids, and sibling target 1 (Palumbo et al., 2015, DOI 10.1177/2041669515604436) is a separate earlier empirical study with different experiments and sample/effect sizes, so report equivalence does not apply.
